note: The inner edge of the sixth circle, where the ground falls away to the seventh. The broken rocks are a landslide, which Virgil accounts for in Canto 12.
The smell of lower Hell, rising from the river of blood and the ditches of the fraudulent. The worse the sin, the fouler the air.

Anastasius II, pope from 496 to 498. He tried to mend a split with the Eastern church and received Photinus, a deacon of Thessalonica from the other side. Medieval tradition made him a heretic for it, which historians now think unjust. Some suspect a confusion with the emperor Anastasius I, who reigned in the same years.

quote: so it doesn't pass in idleness
note: The pause becomes a lesson. This canto has no action: Virgil lays out the map of Hell, and the reasoning behind it.
The seventh, eighth and ninth circles. They are smaller because Hell is a funnel, narrowing as it goes down.

quote: Every evil that earns heaven's hatred
note: Dante's word is malizia, malice: wrong done on purpose to harm someone. The division into force and fraud, with fraud the worse, comes from Cicero's book On Duties.
Animals can be violent, but only a creature with reason can deceive. Fraud turns the gift that makes us human against other people, so it lies deeper in Hell than violence.
The first of the three below: the seventh circle of Hell, Cantos 12–17.

quote: against God, ourselves, and our neighbors
note: The rounds run in the opposite order, from least to worst: violence against a neighbor first, then against oneself, then against God.
A river of boiling blood, where murderers, tyrants and robbers stand sunk to different depths (Canto 12).

The wood of the suicides, whose souls are shut inside thorn trees (Canto 13). With them are those who wrecked their own fortunes, hunted through the wood by dogs. They differ from the spendthrifts of Canto 7: these destroyed their goods as violently as the suicides destroyed their bodies.
The blasphemers, who lie on their backs on burning sand under a rain of fire (Canto 14).

God cannot be struck, but what is his can. Nature is God's work, so an offense against nature, or against the honest labor that follows nature, counts as violence against God. Virgil explains the second point at the end of the canto.
The third and innermost ring of the seventh circle, a desert of burning sand (Cantos 14–17).

Two cities standing for two sins. Sodom, burned by fire from heaven in Genesis 19, gave its name to sodomy (Cantos 15–16). Cahors, in southern France, was so known for its moneylenders that "Cahorsin" was a common word for a usurer (Canto 17).

Fraud has two kinds. To cheat a stranger breaks only the general bond between human beings. To betray someone who had a special reason to trust you breaks that bond too, and is treachery, the worst sin of all.

context: The second of the three, so the eighth circle of Hell. Virgil's list is not in the order of the ditches, and "similar filth" covers the kinds he leaves out.

note: Simony, named for Simon the magician, who offered the apostles money for the power to give the Holy Spirit (Acts 8). Dante finds popes among its sinners in Canto 19.

Dante's word is barattieri: officials who sell public favors and offices, the civil twin of simony (Cantos 21–22). It was the charge the Black Guelphs brought against Dante himself when they banished him.
The particular trust that binds family, fellow citizens, host and guest, lord and follower. Each has its own zone of traitors in the ninth circle.

context: Here the name means Lucifer himself. He sits at the center of the earth, which in Dante's astronomy is the center of the universe and the point farthest from God.

quote: those in the muddy marsh above
note: Dante names four groups from the upper circles, one to a phrase: the wrathful in the marsh (Cantos 7–8), the lustful driven by the wind (Canto 5), the gluttons beaten by the rain (Canto 6), and the misers and spendthrifts who clash and shout insults (Canto 7).
The city of Dis, with its walls glowing from the fire inside. Dante asks why the sinners above are left outside it.

context: The Nicomachean Ethics, "yours" because Dante has studied it so closely. Its seventh book separates the failings Virgil names. The moral plan of Hell rests on Aristotle more than on any list of Christian sins.

note: Incontinence is lack of self-control, giving in to an appetite that is natural in itself: the sins of circles two to five. How the other two terms fit the map is disputed. Many take bestiality to be the violence of the seventh circle and malice the fraud below it.
Outside the walls of Dis, in upper Hell.
Virgil, whose explanations clear Dante's sight as the sun burns off mist.

Lending money at interest. The medieval Church condemned it as a sin, on the ground that money is barren and cannot rightly breed more money. Dante wants to know why it counts as violence against God.
Aristotle's Physics, which says in its second book that art imitates nature. "Art" here means all human skill and making: craft, farming, trade.
Nature is God's child, since it follows his mind. Human work follows nature, so it is nature's child and God's grandchild.

God put Adam in the garden to work it and keep it (Genesis 2:15), and told him after the Fall: "By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread" (3:19). People are meant to live by nature's fruits and their own labor.
He lives neither from what nature grows nor from his own work, but makes money breed money. So he scorns nature and labor both, and through them God.

The constellation Pisces is rising. The sun is in Aries, the next sign, and will follow in about two hours, so it is around four in the morning of Holy Saturday. Virgil cannot see the sky from here. He simply knows.
The Big Dipper, which at this hour lies low in the northwest. Dante's Italian names Caurus, the Latin name of the northwest wind.
